KEY MESSAGE 1...A cold front brings the return of heavy rain and 
gusty winds Sunday night and Monday. Localized flash flooding
possible Monday. 

A potent shortwave trough and anomalous low track across the Ohio 
Valley toward the northeast. A strong 30-45 kt LLJ pushes northward 
into the region tonight helping facilitate lift and advection of an 
anomalous plume of moisture (2-2.5 SD above normal). Positioning 
under the upper level jet, an incoming cold front, and marginal 
instability will provide ample support for widespread heavy rainfall 
Monday. 

Tonight, expect a scattered showers perhaps a weak 
thunderstorm as synoptic ascent/moisture increases ahead of the 
approaching system. Majority of the rain will fall Monday morning 
through Monday evening. This can be divided into two "rounds", 
categorized by timing and prominent hazard. The first "round" will 
be showers and embedded thunderstorms pushing across southern New 
England in the morning through mid-afternoon timeframe. The heaviest 
rain rates will be driven by the location of embedded thunderstorms; 
therefore, the location of the heaviest rainfall will be less 
certain. The HREF shows some isolated low probabilities for rain 
rates 1" or greater during the day Wednesday. The HREF PMM 3 hour 
amounts range from 0.75 to 1.75". With deep moisture/lift efficient 
rainfall is supported. This is where localized to scattered 
flash flooding will be a concern, especially in our areas that 
are still fairly saturated from last week's rain event and the
usual poor drainage areas. The second "round" will be the 
potential for a round of scattered thunderstorms pushing from 
west to east mid afternoon through the evening. There is lower 
confidence in this as it will depend on how much clearing we get
after the first round of showers and thunderstorms. If we can 
get a period of clearing with breaks of sun this will allow the 
atmosphere to destabilize. The unstable/moisture environment 
combined with the incoming cold front and sufficient shear from 
the LLJ would provide an environment support of even a few 
strong to severe thunderstorms if the atmosphere can recover 
from the first round of rain. The primary hazards within any 
stronger storms will be strong downdrafts/gusts and brief heavy 
downpours.

In terms of rain totals, the specific locations of the heaviest 
rainfall will highly depend on where the heavier rates/thunderstorms 
track. Based on global and high-resolution ensemble guidance, many 
areas will see a range of 0.75-2.0" with potential for localized 3". 
HREF ensemble maxes even show potential for close to 4" in localized 
spots. These higher values will be quite localized and will be 
driven by the location of embedded thunderstorms.  

The last thing to address is the gusty winds. With strong winds not 
far from the surface within the strong 30-45 kt LLJ, gusty SW winds 
are likely Monday. Ensemble means show gusts in the 20-35 mph 
range. With the core of the stronger winds positioned across 
east and especially southeast MA, these areas will have the 
greater risk of seeing the higher end of that range. However, 
there is an increasing risk for higher gusts in recent guidance.
A big factor will be if we clear enough from the first push of 
rain to promote mixing, especially in the east/southeast areas 
under the strong core of winds aloft. If winds mix efficiently, 
40 mph gusts are possible in the afternoon in areas (E/SE MA).  

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry and less humid weather returns Tuesday 

Post frontal airmass overspreads the region Tue with good column 
drying, as PWATs plummet to less than an inch. Dry weather, plenty 
of sunshine, dew pts 55-60 and seasonably warm highs of 80-85 
expected. Easily the pick of the week, enjoy! 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Weather pattern quickly becomes unsettled again by 
later Wednesday, continuing late week and into the weekend, with 
periods of showers and storms, noticeably more humid as well. 

Remnant mid level closed low and sub-tropical moisture over the 
southeast states, begins to advect up the eastern seaboard into SNE 
beginning late Wed/Wed night. This moist flow into SNE may persist 
into late week and the weekend, as subtropical ridge develops across 
the western Atlantic, in concert with upstream trough across the 
western Great Lakes. This will translate to an unsettled weather 
pattern for SNE, in the form of periodic showers and thunderstorms 
chances through the period, probably greatest during the 
afternoon/early evening, in response to max heating.
